title: V. The Confession Of A Passionate Heart—“Heels Up”
paragraphs: “Now I get the first half,” said Alyosha.
“The first half, yes. That part was a drama, and it was played out over there. The second part is a tragedy, and it’s being acted out right here.”
“And that second part I don’t understand at all, so far,” said Alyosha.
“And me? Do you think I understand it?”
“Hold on, Dmitri. There’s one important question. Tell me, you were engaged, and you’re still engaged?”

“We didn’t get engaged right away. It was three months after that adventure. The next day I told myself the affair was closed, finished, and there’d be no sequel. Making her an offer seemed caddish to me. And she gave no sign of life herself in the six weeks she stayed on in town, apart from one thing. The day after her visit, her maid slipped round with an envelope addressed to me. I tore it open, and inside was the change from the banknote. Only four thousand five hundred roubles had been needed, but changing the note cost a discount of about two hundred. So all she sent me was about two hundred and sixty. I don’t remember exactly. But there wasn’t a note, not a word of explanation. I went over the packet looking for a pencil mark—n-nothing! So I spent what was left on such an orgy that the new major had to give me a reprimand.

“Then the lieutenant-colonel came up with the battalion money, and everyone was astonished, because nobody believed he still had it untouched. He had barely paid it back when he fell ill and took to his bed. Three weeks later he had softening of the brain, and five days after that he was dead. They buried him with military honors, because he hadn’t had time to get his discharge. Ten days after the funeral Katerina Ivanovna left for Moscow with her aunt and her sister. And on the very day they left (I hadn’t seen them, I didn’t see them off or say goodbye) I got a tiny note, a sheet of thin blue paper, with a single line in pencil: ‘I will write to you. Wait. K.’ That was all.

“I’ll tell you the rest in two words. In Moscow their luck turned as fast as lightning, as unexpectedly as in an Arabian fairy tale. That general’s widow, their nearest relative, suddenly lost the two nieces who were her heiresses and next of kin. Both died of smallpox in the same week. The old lady was crushed with grief. She took Katya in as a daughter, as her one remaining hope, held on to her, and rewrote her will in Katya’s favor. That was for the future, though. For now, she handed her eighty thousand roubles as a marriage portion, to do with as she pleased. She was a hysterical woman. I saw something of her in Moscow, later.

“Then, out of nowhere, four thousand five hundred roubles arrived for me in the post. You can imagine I was speechless. Three days after that came the letter she’d promised. I’ve got it on me now. You must read it. She offers to be my wife. She offers herself to me. ‘I love you madly,’ she writes, ‘even if you don’t love me, never mind. Be my husband. Don’t be afraid. I won’t hamper you in any way. I will be your chattel. I will be the carpet under your feet. I want to love you forever. I want to save you from yourself.’ Alyosha, I’m not fit to repeat those lines in my vulgar words and my vulgar tone, the everlastingly vulgar tone I can never cure myself of. That letter stabs me even now. Do you think I don’t mind? That I don’t mind still? I answered her at once, since I couldn’t possibly go to Moscow. I wrote it in tears. There’s one thing I’ll be ashamed of forever. I brought up her being rich and having a dowry, while I was nothing but a stuck-up beggar! I mentioned money! I should have kept quiet about it, but it slipped out of my pen. Right after that I wrote to Ivan and told him everything I could in a letter of six pages, and I sent him to her. Why are you looking like that? Why are you staring at me? Yes, Ivan fell in love with her. He’s in love with her still. I know it. In the world’s opinion it was a stupid thing to do, but maybe that one stupid thing is what will save all of us now. Oo! Can’t you see how much she thinks of Ivan, how she respects him? When she compares the two of us, do you think she can love a man like me—especially after everything that’s happened here?”
“But I’m sure she loves a man like you, not a man like him.”

“She loves her own _virtue_, not me.” The words burst out of Dmitri, unplanned and almost spiteful. He laughed, but a minute later his eyes flashed, his face went crimson, and he slammed his fist on the table.

“I swear to you, Alyosha,” he cried, in real and bitter anger at himself, “you may not believe me, but as God is holy and Christ is God, I swear it: I smiled at her lofty feelings just now, but I know my soul is a million times baser than hers, and those lofty feelings of hers are as sincere as a heavenly angel’s. That’s the tragedy—I know that for certain. So what if someone shows off a little? Don’t I do it myself? And still I’m sincere, I’m sincere. As for Ivan, I can see how he must be cursing nature now, a man with a mind like his! He sees the preference go to—whom? To what? To a monster who is engaged, with every eye on him, and still can’t hold back his debauchery—and right in front of his fiancée, too! A man like me is the one preferred, and he’s the one turned away. And why? Because a girl wants to throw away her life and her future out of gratitude. It’s ridiculous! I’ve never said a word of this to Ivan, and of course Ivan has never hinted at it to me. But fate will work itself out. The better man will keep his place, and the unworthy one will disappear for ever into his back-alley, his filthy back-alley, his beloved back-alley, where he feels at home and will sink in filth and stink of his own free will and enjoy it. I’ve been talking nonsense. I’m out of words. I’m using them at random, but it will be just as I’ve said. I’ll drown in the back-alley, and she’ll marry Ivan.”

“Stop, Dmitri,” Alyosha broke in again, very worried. “There’s one thing you still haven’t explained: you’re engaged all the same, aren’t you? How can you break it off if she, your fiancée, doesn’t want to?”

“Yes, formally and solemnly engaged. It was settled as soon as I got to Moscow, with great ceremony, with ikons, everything done in style. The general’s widow gave us her blessing and—can you believe it?—congratulated Katya. ‘You’ve chosen well,’ she told her. ‘I can see right through him.’ And—can you believe this too?—she didn’t care for Ivan and barely said hello to him. In Moscow I talked with Katya at length. I told her about myself, sincerely and honorably. She listened to everything.
There was sweet confusion, there were tender words.
Though there were proud words too. She wrung a mighty promise from me to reform. I gave my promise, and now here—”
“What?”
“Why, I called you and dragged you out here today, this very day—remember that!—so I could send you, again today, to Katerina Ivanovna, and—”
“What?”
“To tell her I will never come to see her again. Say, ‘He sends you his compliments.’”
“But is that possible?”
“That’s exactly why I’m sending you in my place: because it can’t be done. How could I say it to her myself?”
“And where will you go?”
“To the back-alley.”
“To Grushenka, then!” Alyosha exclaimed sadly, clasping his hands. “Can Rakitin really have told the truth? I thought you’d only called on her, and that was all.”

“Is a man who’s engaged allowed to make such calls? Is it even possible, with a fiancée like mine, and under the eyes of the whole world? Damn it, I have some honor! The moment I started going to Grushenka, I stopped being engaged, and I stopped being an honest man. I understand that. Why are you looking at me like that? Listen, I went to her first of all to beat her. I’d heard—and now I know for a fact—that the captain, father’s agent, had handed Grushenka an I.O.U. of mine so she could sue me for payment and finish me off. They meant to scare me. So I went to beat her. I’d seen her once in passing before. She doesn’t strike you at first sight. I knew about her old merchant, who’s lying paralyzed and ill now, though he’s leaving her a decent little sum. I knew, too, that she loves money, that she hoards it, that she lends at a wicked rate of interest, that she’s a merciless cheat and swindler. I went to beat her, and I stayed. The storm broke, and it knocked me flat like the plague. I’m plague-stricken still, and I know everything is over, that nothing more will ever come to me. The cycle of the ages is complete. That’s where I stand. And though I’m a beggar, as fate would have it, I happened to have three thousand in my pocket. I drove with Grushenka to Mokroe, twenty-five versts from here. I hired gypsies there, and got champagne, and made all the peasants drunk on it, and all the women and girls. I sent thousands flying. In three days I was stripped bare, but a hero. Do you think the hero got what he was after? Not a sign of it from her. I tell you, that rogue Grushenka has a supple curve running all through her body. You can see it in her little foot, even in her little toe. I saw it, and I kissed it, but that was all, I swear! ‘I’ll marry you if you like,’ she said, ‘but you’re a beggar, you know. Say you won’t beat me and that you’ll let me do whatever I choose, and maybe I’ll marry you.’ She laughed, and she’s laughing still!”
Dmitri sprang to his feet in a kind of fury. All at once he looked drunk. His eyes had suddenly turned bloodshot.
“And do you really mean to marry her?”

“This minute, if she’ll have me. And if she won’t, I’ll hang around anyway. I’ll be the porter at her gate. Alyosha!” he cried. He halted in front of him, took him by the shoulders and shook him hard. “Do you know, you innocent boy, that this is all delirium, senseless delirium? Because there’s a tragedy in it. I’ll tell you something, Alexey. I may be a low man, with low and degraded passions, but Dmitri Karamazov can never be a thief or a pickpocket. Well, then, here it is: I am a thief and a pickpocket. That very morning, just before I went to beat Grushenka, Katerina Ivanovna sent for me. She told me in strict secrecy (why, I don’t know; I suppose she had her reasons) to go to the chief town of the province and mail three thousand roubles to Agafya Ivanovna in Moscow, so that no one here in town would know of it. So I had that three thousand roubles in my pocket when I went to see Grushenka, and that was the money we spent at Mokroe. Later I pretended I’d been to the town, but I never showed her the post office receipt. I said I’d sent the money and would bring her the receipt, and I still haven’t. I forgot it. Now, what do you think you’re going to say to her today? ‘He sends his compliments,’ and she’ll ask you, ‘And the money?’ You could still have told her, ‘He’s a degraded sensualist, a low creature with no control over his passions. He didn’t send your money then. He wasted it, because, like a low brute, he couldn’t restrain himself.’ But you could have added, ‘Still, he isn’t a thief. Here are your three thousand; he sends them back. Send them to Agafya Ivanovna yourself. But he told me to say “he sends his compliments.”’ But as things stand, she’ll ask, ‘But where is the money?’”
“Mitya, you are unhappy, yes! But not as unhappy as you think. Don’t torment yourself to death with despair.”

“What, you think I’ll shoot myself because I can’t find three thousand to pay back? That’s the whole point. I won’t shoot myself. I don’t have the strength for it now. Later, perhaps. For now I’m going to Grushenka. What happens after that, I don’t care.”
“And then what?”
“I’ll be her husband, if she condescends to have me, and when her lovers come I’ll step into the next room. I’ll clean her friends’ galoshes, fan their samovar, run their errands.”

“Katerina Ivanovna will understand all of it,” Alyosha said gravely. “She’ll see how deep this trouble goes, and she’ll forgive you. She has a lofty mind, and she’ll see for herself that no one could be more unhappy than you.”
“She won’t forgive all of it,” said Dmitri with a grin. “There’s something here, brother, that no woman could forgive. Do you know what would be best?”
“What?”
“Paying back the three thousand.”
“But where would we get it? Look, I have two thousand. Ivan will give you another thousand, and that makes three. Take it and pay her back.”

“And when will you have your three thousand in hand? Besides, you’re under age. And you have to—you absolutely have to—carry my farewell to her today, with the money or without it. I can’t drag this out any longer; it’s come to that. Tomorrow will be too late. I’m going to send you to father.”
“To father?”
“Yes, to father first. Ask him for three thousand.”
“But, Mitya, he won’t give it.”
“Of course he won’t! I know that. Alexey, do you know what despair is?”
“Yes.”

“Listen, then. By law he owes me nothing. I’ve had everything from him; I know that. But morally he owes me something, doesn’t he? He started out with twenty-eight thousand of my mother’s money and turned it into a hundred thousand. If he gives me back only three of those twenty-eight thousand, he’ll pull my soul out of hell, and it will make up for a great many of his sins. For that three thousand I give you my solemn word that I’ll put an end to everything, and he’ll never hear of me again. It’s the last time I’ll offer him the chance to be a father. Tell him that God Himself sends him this chance.”
“Mitya, he won’t give it, whatever you say.”

“I know he won’t. I know it perfectly well, and now more than ever. And that’s not all. I know something else. Only a few days ago, perhaps just yesterday, he understood for the first time _in earnest_ (underline _in earnest_) that Grushenka may not be joking after all, and really means to marry me. He knows what she’s like; he knows the cat. So do you imagine he’ll give me money to help that along, when he’s mad about her himself? And that isn’t all, either. I can tell you more than that. I know that for the past five days he’s had three thousand drawn from the bank, changed into notes of a hundred roubles, packed into a big envelope, sealed with five seals and tied crosswise with red tape. You see how well informed I am! On the envelope he’s written: ‘To my angel Grushenka, when she chooses to come to me.’ He scrawled it himself, silently and in secret, and nobody knows the money is there except the valet Smerdyakov, whom he trusts as he trusts himself. So for three or four days now he’s been expecting Grushenka. He hopes she’ll come for the money. He’s sent word to her about it, and she’s sent word back that perhaps she’ll come. And if she does go to the old man, can I marry her afterwards? Now you see why I’m here in secret, and what I’m keeping watch for.”
“For her?”

“Yes, for her. Foma rents a room in the house of these sluts. Foma is from our part of the country; he was a soldier in our regiment. He does odd jobs for them. He’s their watchman at night, and in the daytime he goes shooting grouse. That’s how he makes his living. I’ve moved into his room. Neither he nor the women of the house know the secret, I mean that I’m on watch here.”
“So nobody but Smerdyakov knows?”
“Nobody else. He’ll let me know if she goes to the old man.”
“It was he who told you about the money, then?”

“Yes. It’s a dead secret. Even Ivan knows nothing of the money, or of anything. The old man is sending Ivan to Tchermashnya, a journey of two or three days. A buyer has turned up for the copse, who’ll give eight thousand for the timber. So the old man keeps pressing Ivan to help him out by going to arrange it. It will take him two or three days. That’s what the old man wants, so that Grushenka can come while Ivan is away.”
“So he’s expecting Grushenka today?”

“No, she won’t come today. There are signs. She’s sure not to come,” Mitya suddenly cried. “Smerdyakov thinks so too. Father’s drinking right now. He’s sitting at the table with Ivan. Go to him, Alyosha, and ask for the three thousand.”
“Mitya, dear, what’s wrong with you?” cried Alyosha, leaping up from his seat and staring hard at his brother’s frenzied face. For a moment the thought struck him that Dmitri had gone mad.
“What’s the matter? I’m not insane,” said Dmitri, looking at him intently and earnestly. “Don’t worry. I’m sending you to father, and I know what I’m saying. I believe in miracles.”
“In miracles?”
“In a miracle of Divine Providence. God knows what is in my heart. He sees my despair. He sees the whole picture, and surely He won’t let something awful happen. Alyosha, I believe in miracles. Go!”
“I’m going. Tell me, will you wait here for me?”

“Yes. I know it’ll take a while. You can’t go at him head on. He’s drunk now. I’ll wait three hours—four, five, six, seven. Only remember that you have to go to Katerina Ivanovna today, even at midnight, _with the money or without the money_, and say, ‘He sends his compliments to you.’ I want you to say that very line to her: ‘He sends his compliments to you.’”
“Mitya! And what if Grushenka comes today—or if not today, tomorrow or the day after?”
“Grushenka? I’ll see her. I’ll burst out and stop it.”
“And if—”
“If there’s an if, there will be murder. I couldn’t bear it.”
“Who will be murdered?”
“The old man. I won’t kill her.”
“Brother, what are you saying?”

“Oh, I don’t know.... I don’t know. Maybe I won’t kill him, and maybe I will. I’m afraid that at that moment his face will suddenly become so loathsome to me. I hate his ugly throat, his nose, his eyes, his shameless snigger. I feel a physical disgust. That’s what I’m afraid of. That’s what might be too much for me.”
“I’ll go, Mitya. I believe God will order things for the best, and nothing awful will happen.”
“And I’ll sit here and wait for the miracle. And if it doesn’t happen—”
Alyosha walked off, deep in thought, toward his father’s house.
